findings.title: Favors commerce and business-process language, especially product promotion, purchasing, sales orders, and customer service, though several firings are on incidental word fragments.
Often fires on fees, costs, and other charges in administrative or application instructions; a few unrelated multilingual fragments make this pattern less clean.
Marks sentence-ending periods in ordinary prose, often before the next sentence or section begins.
Marks varied word-internal fragments across otherwise unrelated text, often amid scraped metadata, OCR, or formatting artifacts; no stable semantic pattern is evident.
Primarily OpenShift Enterprise documentation, especially provisioning Ceph RBD persistent volumes and claims; a few weaker hits are unrelated software acronyms or product names.
Code-oriented passages where the marked text is a class, test, library, or other software identifier, often in CamelCase examples; no narrower domain is consistent.
Blog-post taxonomy metadata, especially the CMS footer phrase “Filed under” followed by categories or tags; nearby publishing metadata is a small related extension.
Firings span unrelated uses: comment UI text, reporting verbs, patent filing captions, French function words, and travel attribution.
It often activates on “state” in its condition, jurisdiction, or assertion senses, but also picks up a separate clothing pattern in “dress,” “drest,” and “dressed.”
It activates on digits and separators in numerical strings, including scores, measurements, ranges, statistics, and bibliographic page references.
Fires on fragments of K-containing names and place names (Topeka, Rebekah, Watseka), but also on “Res/Research” in academic citations; these look like separate patterns.
Strongly targets “data” in informational, technical, and privacy contexts, including as the final part of compounds such as “recordsdata.”
Fires on Kraft as a food-company name and in Kraft-derived names, but also on “forces” in Porter’s framework; these appear to be separate lexical patterns.
Primarily marks forms of “force” meaning to compel or cause something, with a smaller related pattern of “empower” meaning to enable or give agency.
Fires on drawing reference numerals attached to named physical components in patent descriptions, especially when identifying parts of a device or embodiment.
No coherent feature emerges: firings span closing parentheses, commas, and unrelated connective or content words in patent and web prose.
No negative-pole examples are provided, so there is no basis for a hypothesis.
Introduces brief qualifying or framing adjuncts, especially parenthetical expressions such as “at first glance,” “in fact,” and “in a sense.”
Fires on opening parentheses that introduce explanatory asides, expansions, citations, or examples; one passage is an outlier involving “the next day.”
Transactional finance and legal deal work, especially acquisitions, due diligence, financing, and securitisation; these are closely related kinds of corporate and asset-finance transactions.
Broad investment-market reporting and investor boilerplate, often about stock, fund, or bond performance, returns, yields, and market movements; some firings are generic words within that prose.
Often marks “Find” phrasing that introduces something being searched for or discovered, especially in directory and service listings; a few matches appear unrelated.
The marked tokens occur in unrelated contexts and show no clear shared pattern or job.
Dash punctuation used to separate quotations from their attributed speaker or source, including em-dash, hyphen, and double-hyphen variants.
The word “to” in the attribution phrase “according to,” introducing a person, publication, or organization as a source.
Detects references to software applications, especially web, mobile, and single-page apps.
The negative examples are heterogeneous, including @ mentions, code terms, and unrelated words, with no clear shared job.
Recognizes mentions of universities, including abbreviations and international spellings; the hit on “univoltine” appears incidental.
Several triggers occur in “College” contexts, but others are unrelated word fragments such as “useful,” “versatile,” and “universal,” with no coherent shared function.
Strongest firings are passages about Asperger syndrome/autism; weaker examples are unrelated words containing common fragments such as “most,” “of,” and “so.”
Most examples concern asphalt/bitumen surfacing, while several others are unrelated technical or proper-name words beginning “asym-,” “asph-,” or “asyn-.”
Mostly marks ecological groupings of vegetation—especially forest or grass stands, but also plant populations and botanical structures in ecological descriptions.
Often marks verbs for visible traits or outcomes (show, display, appear), with some related biological terms for physical action or growth, such as exertion and elongation.
Structural and materials engineering, especially strengthening steel with CFRP and modeling associated debonding, damage, and failure.
Computational and mathematical modeling language across scientific fields, including numerical methods, simulation, fluid dynamics, and optimization.

Centers on Hungarian military history and terminology, especially Honvédség and related names, with a few connected references to Hungarian literature and identity.
No stable pattern is evident: activations include Japanese/Chinese characters, fragments in names, and corner-bracket punctuation, with occasional meanings like discover or send.
Strongly favors generate/development vocabulary and related forms, often in contexts describing production, creation, or growth.
Fires on the Korean road-name suffix 로 in a street address.
Fires mostly on the word patrol and its variants, with a few similarly spelled names such as Paltrow and Patrelle.
